reference.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology / palliative care guidelines
clinicalPearls: Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome of ongoing loss of skeletal muscle, with or without fat loss, that cannot be fully reversed by conventional nutritional support
It is driven by both reduced intake (anorexia) and metabolic derangement, so simply increasing calories does not restore muscle mass
A consensus framework stages it as pre-cachexia, cachexia, and refractory cachexia, which guides how aggressively to intervene
Diagnostic pointers include weight loss over roughly five percent in six months, or lesser weight loss in the setting of low body-mass index or sarcopenia
Systemic inflammation, reflected in raised C-reactive protein and other markers, is central and correlates with worse outcomes
Management is multimodal: nutritional support, resistance exercise where feasible, symptom control of nausea and early satiety, and treatment of the underlying cancer when possible
In refractory cachexia near the end of life the emphasis shifts from reversing weight loss to comfort, and aggressive artificial feeding usually offers little benefit
Family distress about reduced eating is common and benefits from explanation that appetite loss is part of the illness, not a failure of care
reference.pathophysiology: Cancer cachexia results from tumour- and host-derived pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1) and tumour-specific catabolic factors that drive a hypermetabolic, catabolic state. These mediators increase resting energy expenditure, promote skeletal muscle proteolysis and lipolysis, induce insulin resistance, and act centrally to suppress appetite. The net effect is a negative energy and protein balance dominated by muscle wasting that persists despite feeding, distinguishing cachexia from simple starvation in which muscle is relatively spared.
additionalDifferentials: Simple starvation or undernutrition from inadequate intake
Sarcopenia of ageing without underlying malignancy
Depression causing anorexia and weight loss
additionalInvestigations: Documentation of weight trajectory and body-mass index over time
Assessment of muscle mass and function where available
Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and albumin as prognostic indicators
Nutritional assessment including intake and symptoms limiting eating
Screening for reversible contributors such as nausea, constipation, oral problems, and depression
redFlags: Rapid, accelerating weight and muscle loss suggesting progressive or refractory disease
Profound weakness with inability to maintain basic function
Evidence of impending gastrointestinal obstruction limiting intake
Severe deconditioning increasing risk of falls, pressure injury, and infection
reference.prognosis: Cachexia is a marker of advanced disease and independently predicts reduced tolerance of anticancer treatment, poorer quality of life, and shorter survival. Refractory cachexia, typically in the setting of advanced, treatment-unresponsive cancer with a short prognosis, is not reversible, and care goals appropriately shift toward comfort.
pitfalls: Assuming increased calorie provision alone will reverse muscle loss
Pursuing burdensome artificial nutrition in refractory, end-stage disease with no meaningful benefit
Overlooking treatable symptoms that limit intake, such as nausea, constipation, and oral candidiasis
Failing to address family anxiety about the patient not eating
Missing depression as a contributor to anorexia and weight loss
management: Treat the underlying cancer wherever feasible, as this is the only way to reverse the catabolic drive
Deliver multimodal nutritional support led by a dietitian, using oral protein-energy supplementation and enteral feeding when appropriate rather than calories alone
Encourage resistance exercise where the patient is able, to preserve muscle mass and function
Stimulate appetite with a progestational agent or a corticosteroid when anorexia dominates
Control symptoms that limit intake, including nausea, early satiety and constipation, with antiemetics and prokinetics
Stage the syndrome as pre-cachexia, cachexia or refractory cachexia to match the intensity of intervention
Involve palliative care, shifting away from aggressive nutritional intervention once cachexia is refractory in advanced disease
